before.title: Exact adaptive credible coverage in mildly ill-posed Gaussian sequence models
before.statement:
Assume AC and Countable Choice. Fix $p>0$, $C\ge1$, $0<\beta_-<\beta_+<A<\infty$, $R\ge1$, $L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, $\rho\ge2$, $m\in(0,R]$, and $0<\gamma<1$. Let a known positive singular-value sequence satisfy $C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, and observe $X_i=\kappa_i\theta_i+n^{-1/2}\xi_i$ for $i\ge1$, where the fixed truth $\theta=(\theta_i)\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ and the $\xi_i$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. For $\alpha>0$, use the product prior $\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha})$ and its product Gaussian posterior with coordinate mean $n\kappa_iX_i/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$ and variance $(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)^{-1}$. Select $\widehat\alpha_n$ as a Borel global maximizer over $[0,A]$ of the marginal log-likelihood score
$$\ell_n(\alpha;X)=-\frac12\sum_{i\ge1}\left[\log\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right)-\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2X_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}\right],$$
assuming the score series is finite on a Borel data domain of probability one for the truths below and is upper semicontinuous in $\alpha$ there. The $\widehat\alpha_n=0$ branch uses the whole space $\ell^2$ and asserts no posterior probability on $\ell^2$.

For $\theta\in\ell^2$, write $\|\theta\|_2=(\sum_{i\ge1}\theta_i^2)^{1/2}$. For $B\subseteq\ell^2$, define $\operatorname{diam}_{\ell^2}(B)=\sup_{u,v\in B}\|u-v\|_2$, with $\operatorname{diam}_{\ell^2}(\varnothing)=0$.

For $\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]$, let $\Theta_\beta(R)=\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_{i\ge1}i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le R^2\}$ and let $\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consist of those $\theta\in\ell^2$ satisfying $\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2\le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2$ for every integer $N\ge N_0$. Put $\mathcal G_\beta=\Theta_\beta(R)\cap\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\cap\{\theta:\theta_1=0,\ \|\theta\|_2\ge m\}$ and assume the fixed constants make each $\mathcal G_\beta$ nonempty. Does there exist a single graph-measurable data-indexed set rule $C_{n,\gamma}(X)\subseteq\ell^2$, depending only on the known model and class constants and not on $\theta$ or $\beta$, such that on $\widehat\alpha_n>0$ it has posterior mass $\Pi_{\widehat\alpha_n}(C_{n,\gamma}(X)\mid X)\ge1-\gamma$, its uniform frequentist coverage satisfies
$$\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]}\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal G_\beta}\left|P_\theta^{(n)}\{\theta\in C_{n,\gamma}(X)\}-(1-\gamma)\right|\longrightarrow0,$$
and its $\ell^2$-diameter has the no-log rate $n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$ uniformly in the following sense: for every $\eta>0$ there is $K_\eta<\infty$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]}\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal G_\beta}P_\theta^{(n)}\left\{\operatorname{diam}_{\ell^2}(C_{n,\gamma}(X))>K_\eta n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}\right\}\le\eta?$$

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$,
an inflation factor $L\ge0$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}.$$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1,$$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}).$$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}.$$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$\ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right].$$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$\widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, a sequence
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, a truth
$\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$, where $\mathbb N_+=\{1,2,\ldots\}$,
and $0<\alpha<\infty$. Consider the prior
$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha})$ and observations
$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i$, where the $Z_i$ are independent
$N(0,1)$. Denote their sampling law by $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$ and write
$\ell^2=\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$ throughout this lemma. For
$n\ge3$ and $0<\alpha\le A_n$, these are the model and prior in
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]]; the present
fixed-$\alpha$ calculation requires no maximization domain or selector. Put
$r=1+2\alpha$. Then the product prior is supported on $\ell^2$, and its
posterior kernel under the prior-predictive law $Q_{n,\alpha}$ is the product
of the coordinate laws
$$N\!\left( \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2}, \frac{1}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right),\qquad i\ge1,$$
For $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost every observation $x$, this same kernel is
supported on $\ell^2$, and its posterior mean belongs to $\ell^2$.

Let $Q_{n,\alpha}$ be the prior-predictive law of $X$ under this prior and
let $Q_{n,0}=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$. Then $Q_{n,\alpha}\ll Q_{n,0}$
and
$$\log\frac{dQ_{n,\alpha}}{dQ_{n,0}}(x) =-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^r}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right] =\ell_n(\alpha;x).$$
The density identity and absolute convergence hold $Q_{n,0}$-almost surely.
The same displayed score series also converges absolutely
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost surely; this latter assertion does not identify a
version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

Use the Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$,
$\rho\ge2$, and $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Assume that
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ and
$\theta_{0,1}=0$. Then there is a finite inflation constant $L>0$,
depending only on the fixed model and class parameters, such that
$$\inf_{\substack{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\\ \theta_{0,1}=0}} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_n(L)\} \longrightarrow1.$$
This is conservative frequentist coverage tending to one, not exact
asymptotic coverage $1-\gamma$. The source also allows a sequence of caps
$A_n>0$ satisfying, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$A_n\le \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}.$$
In that case there is a constant $K_{\mathrm{infl}}>0$, depending only on the
fixed model and class parameters and not on $n$, such that the same coverage
conclusion holds for any deterministic inflation sequence satisfying
$$L_n\ge K_{\mathrm{infl}}(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Use the inverse Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and $\kappa_i^2\in[C^{-2}i^{-2p},C^2i^{-2p}]$.
Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. Let
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ with $\theta_{0,1}=0$.
For $n\ge3$ and $\alpha\in[0,A]$, put
$$N_{n,\alpha}=n^{1/(1+2\alpha+2p)},\qquad h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)= \frac{1+2\alpha+2p}{N_{n,\alpha}\log n} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2 i^{1+2\alpha}(\log i)\theta_{0,i}^2} {(i^{1+2\alpha+2p}+n)^2}.$$
Define
$$\underline\alpha_n= \inf\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\ge(16C^8)^{-1}\}, \qquad \overline\alpha_n= \sup\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\le8C^8\},$$
with the source conventions $\inf\varnothing=A$ and $\sup\varnothing=0$.
Then the source bracket result is
$$\inf_{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho),\,\theta_{0,1}=0} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)} \bigl(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n\le\overline\alpha_n\bigr) \longrightarrow1.$$
More generally, the same conclusion holds with $A=A_n$ whenever
$$0<A_n\le\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$. Uniformly in the polished-tail class, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\frac{n^{-2\underline\alpha_n/(1+2\underline\alpha_n+2p)}}{n^{-2\overline\alpha_n/(1+2\overline\alpha_n+2p)}}\le\left[128C^{16}\{4+36L_0\rho^{1+2A_n}\}\right]^{1+2p}.$$
In particular, for fixed $A$ the two rates are uniformly comparable. The lower bracket alone is valid uniformly over arbitrary $\theta_0\in\ell^2$, using the same definition of $\underline\alpha_n$ and the same procedure/domain hypotheses:
$$\inf_{\theta_0\in\ell^2}P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n)\longrightarrow1.$$

Use the defined inverse Gaussian sequence procedure with fixed $p,C,L_0,N_0,\rho$ and $0<A=A_n\le\sqrt{\log n}/(4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)})$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Write
$$r_\alpha=1+2\alpha+2p,\quad s_\alpha=1+2\alpha,\quad N_\alpha=n^{1/r_\alpha},\quad V_\alpha=N_\alpha\log N_\alpha,\quad f_\alpha(i)=\frac{n^2i^{s_\alpha}\log i}{(i^{r_\alpha}+n)^2},\quad S_\alpha=\sum_i f_\alpha(i)\theta_i^2,\quad h_\alpha=S_\alpha/V_\alpha.$$
The likelihood has a continuous derivative $M_n$ on $[0,A]$, with the derivative at zero interpreted from the right. Let $Q_n=M_n-E_\theta M_n$. Uniformly over $\theta\in\Theta_{\rm pt}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$,
$$E_\theta\sup_{0\le\alpha\le A}\frac{|Q_n(\alpha)|}{V_\alpha(1+h_\alpha)}\le\frac{K\{1+A L_0\rho^{1+2A}\log n\}}{\sqrt{N_A}}\longrightarrow0.$$
For all sufficiently large $n$, all $0\le a\le b\le A$, and every such truth,
$$h_a\le(4+36L_0\rho^{1+2b})\frac{N_b}{N_a}h_b.$$
For every $\theta\in\ell^2$, the expectation satisfies
$$\frac{E_\theta M_n(\alpha)}{V_\alpha}\ge\frac1{8C^4}-C^4h_\alpha,\qquad \frac{E_\theta M_n(\alpha)}{V_\alpha}\le3C^4-C^{-4}h_\alpha.$$
Finally, for arbitrary $\theta\in\ell^2$ and every deterministic interval $[0,c]\subseteq[0,A]$ on which $h_\alpha\le H$, where $H$ is fixed, one has
$$E_\theta\sup_{0\le\alpha\le c}\frac{|Q_n(\alpha)|}{V_\alpha}\le\frac{K_H(1+A\log n)}{\sqrt{N_A}}\longrightarrow0.$$
Constants do not depend on $n,A,\theta$. Fixed finite $A$ is allowed by the eventual cap.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2.$$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

derivations.claim: Fix the inflation $L\ge1$ in [F2], depending only on the known constants. Let $B_n=\widehat C_n(L)$, including its whole-space zero-selector branch. With $U=\bigcup_{\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]}\mathcal G_\beta$, [F2] gives $\epsilon_n:=\sup_{\theta\in U}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\theta\notin B_n\}\to0$. This is uniform because $U$ is a subset of the single polished-tail class in that theorem. This step claims conservative coverage only.

The random positive-selector posterior is supported on $\ell^2$ on a single Borel domain, not merely on a separate almost-sure domain for each fixed hyperparameter. Indeed intersect the supplied score domain with
$$T_n=\left\{x:\sum_i n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2/i^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every square-summable truth the expectation of this nonnegative sum is
$$n^2\sum_i\kappa_i^4\theta_i^2/i^2+n\sum_i\kappa_i^2/i^2<\infty.$$
Thus $T_n$ is Borel and has probability one under every such truth. For every $x\in T_n$ and every $a\ge0$, the squared posterior mean is bounded by that same sum, since $i^{1+2a}+n\kappa_i^2\ge i$. For every $a>0$ the variance trace is finite. Hence all positive-parameter posterior laws at these data are supported on $\ell^2$, including the selected law. Extend the selector by zero and use the whole space outside this common declared domain. This changes none of the sampling probabilities and asserts no posterior on the zero branch.

We verify the diameter rate uniformly in $\beta$, rather than import a pointwise Sobolev assertion. Write $q_a=1+2a+2p$, $N_a=n^{1/q_a}$, and $d=\beta-a\ge0$. In the score $h_n(a;\theta)$ of [F3], put $e_i=i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2$, so $\sum_i e_i\le R^2$. For $i\le N_a$, the multiplier of $e_i$ is at most
$$\frac{i^{1-2d}\log i}{N_a\log N_a}\le N_a^{-\min(1,2d)}.$$
If $1-2d\ge0$, bound both powers and logarithms by their values at $N_a$; otherwise use $i^{1-2d}\le1$. For $i>N_a$, the multiplier is at most
$$\frac{N_a^{2q_a}}{N_a\log N_a}i^{-1-2a-4p-2\beta}\log i\le N_a^{-2d}.$$
The last function of $i$ is decreasing for $i\ge N_a$ once $n$ is uniformly large, since its negative power has exponent at least $1+4p$. Both ranges therefore give
$$h_n(a;\theta)\le R^2N_a^{-\min(1,2(\beta-a))}.$$
These bounds hold simultaneously for $0\le a\le\beta$, every $\beta$ in the fixed compact interval, and every $\theta\in\Theta_\beta(R)$.

Choose a fixed $D>0$ with $R^2\exp\{-2D/(1+2\beta_++2p)\}<t$. For all sufficiently large $n$, put $a_{n,\beta}=\beta-D/\log n\ge\beta_-/2$. For every $0\le a\le a_{n,\beta}$, step 2.1 makes $h_n(a;\theta)<t$: here $\min(1,2(\beta-a))\log N_a\ge2D/(1+2\beta_++2p)$ when $\log n\ge2D$. Consequently $\underline\alpha_n\ge a_{n,\beta}$, including the empty-threshold convention $\underline\alpha_n=A$. The uniform lower bracket [F3] yields
$$\sup_{\beta,\theta\in\mathcal G_\beta}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\widehat\alpha_n<a_{n,\beta}\}\longrightarrow0.$$
In particular $\delta_n:=\sup_{\theta\in U}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\widehat\alpha_n=0\}\to0$.

Uniformly for $a\in[\beta_-/2,A]$, split the posterior variance trace at $N_a$. Below that cutoff use $v_i(a)\le C^2i^{2p}/n$; above it use $v_i(a)\le i^{-1-2a}$. Summation and an integral comparison give
$$\sum_i v_i(a)\le K n^{-2a/q_a},$$
where $K$ depends only on the fixed constants (the tail factor $1/(2a)$ is uniformly bounded). Markov's inequality applied to the centered posterior squared norm bounds its $(1-\gamma)$ norm quantile by $\sqrt{K/\gamma}\,n^{-a/q_a}$. The variances, hence the norm quantile, decrease with $a$ by coupling all centered coordinates with the same standard normals. On the event of step 2.2, the selected radius is therefore at most $\sqrt{K/\gamma}\,n^{-a_{n,\beta}/q_{a_{n,\beta}}}$. The derivative of $a/q_a$ is $(1+2p)/q_a^2\le1/(1+2p)$, so this is at most $K' n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$ with one $K'$ for the full compact $\beta$ interval. Thus outside an event of uniformly vanishing probability, $\operatorname{diam}(B_n)\le2LK'n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$. This includes the uniformly negligible infinite-diameter zero-selector branch.

Put $H=\{u\in\ell^2:u_1=0\}$, $Z_n=\{\widehat\alpha_n=0\}$ and $E_n=\{\sqrt nX_1\le\Phi^{-1}(1-\gamma)\}$. Define
$$C_n=\begin{cases}\ell^2,&Z_n,\\B_n,&Z_n^c\cap E_n,\\B_n\setminus H,&Z_n^c\cap E_n^c.\end{cases}$$
For $n<3$ one may use $\ell^2$. The positive-selector posterior's first-coordinate variance is $(1+n\kappa_1^2)^{-1}>0$, so it assigns $H$ mass zero for every data point of the declared domain, even though the hyperparameter is data-selected. Since $L\ge1$, $B_n$ has posterior mass at least $1-\gamma$; deleting $H$ preserves that mass. On $Z_n$ the specified whole-space convention is retained.

This is one rule independent of $\theta$ and $\beta$. Its graph is Borel: the coordinate posterior means and selector are Borel, and the squared norm is the limit of its finite coordinate sums. For completeness, on a fixed countable standard-normal product space the map $(a,z)\mapsto\sum_i v_i(a)z_i^2$ is nonnegative Borel. Integrating its threshold indicators gives a Borel distribution function in $(a,s)$. Its quantile is Borel, by taking the infimum of positive rational radii whose distribution function is at least $1-\gamma$; right continuity ensures this quantile has the required posterior mass. The centered norm has a positive finite quantile: it is finite by its finite second moment and has no atom at zero because its first coordinate is nondegenerate. Thus the radius is positive. Deleting the closed codimension-one hyperplane leaves a dense subset of any positive-radius ball: perturb a point toward the center if necessary and then a sufficiently small amount along the first coordinate. Hence $B_n\setminus H$ has the same diameter $2Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ as $B_n$. Diameter is consequently an extended Borel random variable, equal to this expression off $Z_n$ and infinity on $Z_n$.

Every allowed truth lies in $H$ and has $P_\theta^{(n)}(E_n)=1-\gamma$ exactly, since $\theta_1=0$. Its coverage equals
$$P_\theta(Z_n)+P_\theta(Z_n^c\cap E_n\cap\{\theta\in B_n\}).$$
Subtracting $P_\theta(E_n)$ leaves
$$P_\theta(Z_n\cap E_n^c)-P_\theta(Z_n^c\cap E_n\cap\{\theta\notin B_n\}).$$
Its absolute value is at most $\delta_n+\epsilon_n\to0$ uniformly over both suprema in the question. No independence among $E_n$, the selector and $B_n$ is used. Also $C_n\subseteq B_n$ on every branch, so step 3.1 proves the requested diameter statement, in fact with limiting supremum zero for one sufficiently large fixed diameter constant. The nonzero lower norm bound $m$ is retained and needs no additional argument. This answers the unchanged unrestricted existence question affirmatively. It does not identify the constructed sets as balls or attribute this null-deletion construction to the cited literature.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$,
an inflation factor $L\ge0$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}.$$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1,$$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}).$$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}.$$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$\ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right].$$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$\widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, a sequence
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, a truth
$\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$, where $\mathbb N_+=\{1,2,\ldots\}$,
and $0<\alpha<\infty$. Consider the prior
$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha})$ and observations
$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i$, where the $Z_i$ are independent
$N(0,1)$. Denote their sampling law by $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$ and write
$\ell^2=\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$ throughout this lemma. For
$n\ge3$ and $0<\alpha\le A_n$, these are the model and prior in
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]]; the present
fixed-$\alpha$ calculation requires no maximization domain or selector. Put
$r=1+2\alpha$. Then the product prior is supported on $\ell^2$, and its
posterior kernel under the prior-predictive law $Q_{n,\alpha}$ is the product
of the coordinate laws
$$N\!\left( \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2}, \frac{1}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right),\qquad i\ge1,$$
For $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost every observation $x$, this same kernel is
supported on $\ell^2$, and its posterior mean belongs to $\ell^2$.

Let $Q_{n,\alpha}$ be the prior-predictive law of $X$ under this prior and
let $Q_{n,0}=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$. Then $Q_{n,\alpha}\ll Q_{n,0}$
and
$$\log\frac{dQ_{n,\alpha}}{dQ_{n,0}}(x) =-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^r}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right] =\ell_n(\alpha;x).$$
The density identity and absolute convergence hold $Q_{n,0}$-almost surely.
The same displayed score series also converges absolutely
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost surely; this latter assertion does not identify a
version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

Use the Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$,
$\rho\ge2$, and $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Assume that
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ and
$\theta_{0,1}=0$. Then there is a finite inflation constant $L>0$,
depending only on the fixed model and class parameters, such that
$$\inf_{\substack{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\\ \theta_{0,1}=0}} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_n(L)\} \longrightarrow1.$$
This is conservative frequentist coverage tending to one, not exact
asymptotic coverage $1-\gamma$. The source also allows a sequence of caps
$A_n>0$ satisfying, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$A_n\le \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}.$$
In that case there is a constant $K_{\mathrm{infl}}>0$, depending only on the
fixed model and class parameters and not on $n$, such that the same coverage
conclusion holds for any deterministic inflation sequence satisfying
$$L_n\ge K_{\mathrm{infl}}(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Use the inverse Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and $\kappa_i^2\in[C^{-2}i^{-2p},C^2i^{-2p}]$.
Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. Let
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ with $\theta_{0,1}=0$.
For $n\ge3$ and $\alpha\in[0,A]$, put
$$N_{n,\alpha}=n^{1/(1+2\alpha+2p)},\qquad h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)= \frac{1+2\alpha+2p}{N_{n,\alpha}\log n} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2 i^{1+2\alpha}(\log i)\theta_{0,i}^2} {(i^{1+2\alpha+2p}+n)^2}.$$
Define
$$\underline\alpha_n= \inf\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\ge(16C^8)^{-1}\}, \qquad \overline\alpha_n= \sup\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\le8C^8\},$$
with the source conventions $\inf\varnothing=A$ and $\sup\varnothing=0$.
Then the source bracket result is
$$\inf_{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho),\,\theta_{0,1}=0} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)} \bigl(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n\le\overline\alpha_n\bigr) \longrightarrow1.$$
More generally, the same conclusion holds with $A=A_n$ whenever
$$0<A_n\le\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$. Uniformly in the polished-tail class, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\frac{n^{-2\underline\alpha_n/(1+2\underline\alpha_n+2p)}}{n^{-2\overline\alpha_n/(1+2\overline\alpha_n+2p)}}\le\left[128C^{16}\{4+36L_0\rho^{1+2A_n}\}\right]^{1+2p}.$$
In particular, for fixed $A$ the two rates are uniformly comparable. The lower bracket alone is valid uniformly over arbitrary $\theta_0\in\ell^2$, using the same definition of $\underline\alpha_n$ and the same procedure/domain hypotheses:
$$\inf_{\theta_0\in\ell^2}P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n)\longrightarrow1.$$

Use the defined inverse Gaussian sequence procedure with fixed $p,C,L_0,N_0,\rho$ and $0<A=A_n\le\sqrt{\log n}/(4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)})$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Write
$$r_\alpha=1+2\alpha+2p,\quad s_\alpha=1+2\alpha,\quad N_\alpha=n^{1/r_\alpha},\quad V_\alpha=N_\alpha\log N_\alpha,\quad f_\alpha(i)=\frac{n^2i^{s_\alpha}\log i}{(i^{r_\alpha}+n)^2},\quad S_\alpha=\sum_i f_\alpha(i)\theta_i^2,\quad h_\alpha=S_\alpha/V_\alpha.$$
The likelihood has a continuous derivative $M_n$ on $[0,A]$, with the derivative at zero interpreted from the right. Let $Q_n=M_n-E_\theta M_n$. Uniformly over $\theta\in\Theta_{\rm pt}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$,
$$E_\theta\sup_{0\le\alpha\le A}\frac{|Q_n(\alpha)|}{V_\alpha(1+h_\alpha)}\le\frac{K\{1+A L_0\rho^{1+2A}\log n\}}{\sqrt{N_A}}\longrightarrow0.$$
For all sufficiently large $n$, all $0\le a\le b\le A$, and every such truth,
$$h_a\le(4+36L_0\rho^{1+2b})\frac{N_b}{N_a}h_b.$$
For every $\theta\in\ell^2$, the expectation satisfies
$$\frac{E_\theta M_n(\alpha)}{V_\alpha}\ge\frac1{8C^4}-C^4h_\alpha,\qquad \frac{E_\theta M_n(\alpha)}{V_\alpha}\le3C^4-C^{-4}h_\alpha.$$
Finally, for arbitrary $\theta\in\ell^2$ and every deterministic interval $[0,c]\subseteq[0,A]$ on which $h_\alpha\le H$, where $H$ is fixed, one has
$$E_\theta\sup_{0\le\alpha\le c}\frac{|Q_n(\alpha)|}{V_\alpha}\le\frac{K_H(1+A\log n)}{\sqrt{N_A}}\longrightarrow0.$$
Constants do not depend on $n,A,\theta$. Fixed finite $A$ is allowed by the eventual cap.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2.$$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

derivations.claim: Fix the inflation $L\ge1$ in [F2], depending only on the known constants. Let $B_n=\widehat C_n(L)$, including its whole-space zero-selector branch. With $U=\bigcup_{\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]}\mathcal G_\beta$, [F2] gives $\epsilon_n:=\sup_{\theta\in U}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\theta\notin B_n\}\to0$. This is uniform because $U$ is a subset of the single polished-tail class in that theorem. This step claims conservative coverage only.

The random positive-selector posterior is supported on $\ell^2$ on a single Borel domain, not merely on a separate almost-sure domain for each fixed hyperparameter. Indeed intersect the supplied score domain with
$$T_n=\left\{x:\sum_i n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2/i^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every square-summable truth the expectation of this nonnegative sum is
$$n^2\sum_i\kappa_i^4\theta_i^2/i^2+n\sum_i\kappa_i^2/i^2<\infty.$$
Thus $T_n$ is Borel and has probability one under every such truth. For every $x\in T_n$ and every $a\ge0$, the squared posterior mean is bounded by that same sum, since $i^{1+2a}+n\kappa_i^2\ge i$. For every $a>0$ the variance trace is finite. Hence all positive-parameter posterior laws at these data are supported on $\ell^2$, including the selected law. Extend the selector by zero and use the whole space outside this common declared domain. This changes none of the sampling probabilities and asserts no posterior on the zero branch.

We verify the diameter rate uniformly in $\beta$, rather than import a pointwise Sobolev assertion. Write $q_a=1+2a+2p$, $N_a=n^{1/q_a}$, and $d=\beta-a\ge0$. In the score $h_n(a;\theta)$ of [F3], put $e_i=i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2$, so $\sum_i e_i\le R^2$. For $i\le N_a$, the multiplier of $e_i$ is at most
$$\frac{i^{1-2d}\log i}{N_a\log N_a}\le N_a^{-\min(1,2d)}.$$
If $1-2d\ge0$, bound both powers and logarithms by their values at $N_a$; otherwise use $i^{1-2d}\le1$. For $i>N_a$, the multiplier is at most
$$\frac{N_a^{2q_a}}{N_a\log N_a}i^{-1-2a-4p-2\beta}\log i\le N_a^{-2d}.$$
The last function of $i$ is decreasing for $i\ge N_a$ once $n$ is uniformly large, since its negative power has exponent at least $1+4p$. Both ranges therefore give
$$h_n(a;\theta)\le R^2N_a^{-\min(1,2(\beta-a))}.$$
These bounds hold simultaneously for $0\le a\le\beta$, every $\beta$ in the fixed compact interval, and every $\theta\in\Theta_\beta(R)$.

Choose a fixed $D>0$ with $R^2\exp\{-2D/(1+2\beta_++2p)\}<t$. For all sufficiently large $n$, put $a_{n,\beta}=\beta-D/\log n\ge\beta_-/2$. For every $0\le a\le a_{n,\beta}$, step 2.1 makes $h_n(a;\theta)<t$: here $\min(1,2(\beta-a))\log N_a\ge2D/(1+2\beta_++2p)$ when $\log n\ge2D$. Consequently $\underline\alpha_n\ge a_{n,\beta}$, including the empty-threshold convention $\underline\alpha_n=A$. The uniform lower bracket [F3] yields
$$\sup_{\beta,\theta\in\mathcal G_\beta}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\widehat\alpha_n<a_{n,\beta}\}\longrightarrow0.$$
In particular $\delta_n:=\sup_{\theta\in U}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\widehat\alpha_n=0\}\to0$.

Uniformly for $a\in[\beta_-/2,A]$, split the posterior variance trace at $N_a$. Below that cutoff use $v_i(a)\le C^2i^{2p}/n$; above it use $v_i(a)\le i^{-1-2a}$. Summation and an integral comparison give
$$\sum_i v_i(a)\le K n^{-2a/q_a},$$
where $K$ depends only on the fixed constants (the tail factor $1/(2a)$ is uniformly bounded). Markov's inequality applied to the centered posterior squared norm bounds its $(1-\gamma)$ norm quantile by $\sqrt{K/\gamma}\,n^{-a/q_a}$. The variances, hence the norm quantile, decrease with $a$ by coupling all centered coordinates with the same standard normals. On the event of step 2.2, the selected radius is therefore at most $\sqrt{K/\gamma}\,n^{-a_{n,\beta}/q_{a_{n,\beta}}}$. The derivative of $a/q_a$ is $(1+2p)/q_a^2\le1/(1+2p)$, so this is at most $K' n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$ with one $K'$ for the full compact $\beta$ interval. Thus outside an event of uniformly vanishing probability, $\operatorname{diam}(B_n)\le2LK'n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$. This includes the uniformly negligible infinite-diameter zero-selector branch.

Put $H=\{u\in\ell^2:u_1=0\}$, $Z_n=\{\widehat\alpha_n=0\}$ and $E_n=\{\sqrt nX_1\le\Phi^{-1}(1-\gamma)\}$. Define
$$C_n=\begin{cases}\ell^2,&Z_n,\\B_n,&Z_n^c\cap E_n,\\B_n\setminus H,&Z_n^c\cap E_n^c.\end{cases}$$
For $n<3$ one may use $\ell^2$. The positive-selector posterior's first-coordinate variance is $(1+n\kappa_1^2)^{-1}>0$, so it assigns $H$ mass zero for every data point of the declared domain, even though the hyperparameter is data-selected. Since $L\ge1$, $B_n$ has posterior mass at least $1-\gamma$; deleting $H$ preserves that mass. On $Z_n$ the specified whole-space convention is retained.

This is one rule independent of $\theta$ and $\beta$. Its graph is Borel: the coordinate posterior means and selector are Borel, and the squared norm is the limit of its finite coordinate sums. For completeness, on a fixed countable standard-normal product space the map $(a,z)\mapsto\sum_i v_i(a)z_i^2$ is nonnegative Borel. Integrating its threshold indicators gives a Borel distribution function in $(a,s)$. Its quantile is Borel, by taking the infimum of positive rational radii whose distribution function is at least $1-\gamma$; right continuity ensures this quantile has the required posterior mass. The centered norm has a positive finite quantile: it is finite by its finite second moment and has no atom at zero because its first coordinate is nondegenerate. Thus the radius is positive. Deleting the closed codimension-one hyperplane leaves a dense subset of any positive-radius ball: perturb a point toward the center if necessary and then a sufficiently small amount along the first coordinate. Hence $B_n\setminus H$ has the same diameter $2Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ as $B_n$. Diameter is consequently an extended Borel random variable, equal to this expression off $Z_n$ and infinity on $Z_n$.

Every allowed truth lies in $H$ and has $P_\theta^{(n)}(E_n)=1-\gamma$ exactly, since $\theta_1=0$. Its coverage equals
$$P_\theta(Z_n)+P_\theta(Z_n^c\cap E_n\cap\{\theta\in B_n\}).$$
Subtracting $P_\theta(E_n)$ leaves
$$P_\theta(Z_n\cap E_n^c)-P_\theta(Z_n^c\cap E_n\cap\{\theta\notin B_n\}).$$
Its absolute value is at most $\delta_n+\epsilon_n\to0$ uniformly over both suprema in the question. No independence among $E_n$, the selector and $B_n$ is used. Also $C_n\subseteq B_n$ on every branch, so step 3.1 proves the requested diameter statement, in fact with limiting supremum zero for one sufficiently large fixed diameter constant. The nonzero lower norm bound $m$ is retained and needs no additional argument. This answers the unchanged unrestricted existence question affirmatively. It does not identify the constructed sets as balls or attribute this null-deletion construction to the cited literature.
